To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

CD133 expression (as detected by AC133) cannot be detected in benign or malignant prostate cells by either flow cytometry or immunohistochemistry, and that CD49f is an efficient marker of monolayer and sphere colony forming cells of the benign and malignant human prostate.
CD49f is an efficient marker of monolayer and sphere colony-forming cells in the benign and prostate cancer prostate, and that CD133 expression (using AC133 clone) is absent in benign prostate.
CD49f is a superior stem cell marker for prostate cells, compared to CD44 and CD44, and that the CD133 (AC133) clone does not identify CD133+ cells in the benign and cancerous prostate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a cell culture system to study prostate stem cells and prostate cancer stem cells.
prostate stem cells, which are cells that have the capacity to self-renew and give rise to all cell types of prostate.
the isolation and characterization of stem cells from the benign and malignant human prostate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CD49f is the best marker for prostate stem cells.
CD44, CD133, CD49f and CD90 are not the most efficient markers to isolate putative prostate stem/progenitor cells, and that CD44 and CD90 are less efficient than CD133 and CD49f, respectively.
CD49f is the best marker for stem-like cells in prostate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CD133 is not a useful marker for prostate stem cells and CD49f is an efficient marker for monolayer- or spheroid CFCs of both benign and malignant prostates.
CD49f is a more efficient marker for selecting stem cells from the prostate than CD44 or CD133.
CD49f is an efficient marker of monolayer and 3D spheroid CFCs of benign and malignant human prostate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CD49f+ cells are the best marker for stem cells in the prostate.
CD49f is an efficient marker of stem-like cells of the benign and malignant human prostate, but that the CD49f+ population is heterogeneous and contains both stem-like and non-stem-like cells.
CD133 expression in the prostate is not consistent with the expression of CD133 in other organs.
